messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 79-year-old African American man, divorced, who has worked for the past several years as a warehouse worker — a role he took on late in life partly for the physical routine it provides and partly, as he has since acknowledged, because the noise and activity of the loading dock kept him from sitting too long with himself. He was referred for psychological assessment following a conversation with his primary care physician, who noted that Kwame had been drinking more heavily than usual and had recently been involved in a verbal altercation with a supervisor that nearly cost him his job.

The events that shaped Kwame's inner life stretch back more than seven decades, to a rural setting in West Africa where he spent his early childhood before emigrating with relatives as a young adolescent. What he carries from that time is not a clean narrative but something more fractured — impressions, sensations, silences. What he can piece together, in disconnected fragments that refuse to form a coherent whole, is that his father was a violent man and that his mother bore the consequences of that violence repeatedly, sometimes in the open air behind their home, where the smell of palm wine and fermented drink often preceded what would follow. Kwame remembers the sounds more than the images: doors thrown open or slammed shut as the prelude to something terrible, his mother's voice, the particular quality of outdoor air in those moments — humid, green, alive with insects — that became inseparable from dread. When he tries now, deliberately, to retrieve a clear picture of what happened, he finds the memory will not come to him that way. It resists direct examination. What arrives instead, without warning and without a face attached, is the feeling — a cold, expansive terror that seems to belong to no particular moment and yet to every moment at once.

For most of his adult life, Kwame managed. He worked, raised children with a woman he later divorced, built a life in the United States through sheer physical persistence. But in recent years, as his world has quieted and his children have grown distant — a consequence, at least in part, of the arguments and provocations that have become a recurring pattern in his relationships — the feelings have grown harder to outrun. He has come to believe that being alone is genuinely dangerous, not in any way he could articulate precisely, but in the sense that silence and solitude seem to open a door inside him that he cannot close again once it is open. He keeps himself surrounded by people as a result — at the warehouse, at the bar, at the homes of neighbors he barely knows — filling every available hour with the presence of others.

The warehouse itself has become a complicated place. The loading dock opens onto a scrubby patch of land at the edge of the property, and on warm mornings, when the air carries the smell of earth and wet grass, Kwame finds himself stopping at the threshold, unable to say why his chest has tightened or why the ordinary outdoor smell of the place feels suddenly charged with something he cannot name. He turns back inside without acknowledging it to anyone. Doors are another matter. The warehouse is full of them — heavy rolling doors, fire exits that bang shut in the wind — and each sudden slam lands in his body before his mind has registered anything at all. He has snapped at coworkers for less. The altercation with his supervisor began, by his own account, with a door.

Kwame drinks in the evenings, and he is aware, in a way he finds both shameful and confusing, that the smell of alcohol is one of the things that most unsettles him — that the very substance he reaches for carries within it the sensory residue of what he is trying not to feel. He has not said this plainly, but it surfaces in the way he describes his evenings: restless, unresolved, waking in the night with his heart already racing and no image to account for it.

What finally brought him to seek help was the near-loss of his job — the one structure that still organizes his days. What he fears most is that there is nothing coherent left to remember, and therefore nothing that can be helped. What he hopes, more quietly, is that someone might prove him wrong.
